title: fastpath-chunking-lab-snapshot
summary: Quick lab-snapshot comparing three response strategies under mixed chat+embedding workload: direct fastpath, small-chunk streaming, and multiplexed bulk. Focus on p50/p90/p99, cost per 1k queries, and behavior during short microbursts.
content:
Objective:
Run a compact, repeatable set of microbench experiments to surface tradeoffs between latency SLOs and unit cost for three serving strategies we keep discussing in product and infra: direct fastpath (FP), chunked streaming (CS), and multiplexed bulk (MB). This doc records the harness, raw summary numbers, lightweight charts (ASCII), observations, and recommended next steps.

Test harness and workload:
- Hardware: 1 x A10G-equivalent node (GPU inference fleet slot), single model (open LLM vX, 16k context, FP16 qkv).
- Traffic shapes:
  1) Steady 100 qps sustained for 10 minutes (baseline).
  2) Microburst: 5s ramp to 1,000 qps (single short spike) then back to baseline.
  3) Sessionized chat: average session 400 tokens, arrival Poisson at 20 sessions/s (bursty interleaving).
- Payload mix: 70% chat-generation (avg 120 tokens), 30% embeddings (short requests).
- Cache: KV cache enabled for FP/CS/MB with identical TTL and warm prefix distribution.
- Measurement: p50/p90/p99 tail (ms) measured at client-observed completion; cost estimated from amortized GPU-seconds per request scaled to $/1k queries using internal cost model.

Modes under test (short):
- FP (direct fastpath): route each request to minimal decode pipeline, low software stack overhead, minimal batching. Emphasizes low p50.
- CS (chunked streaming): stream output in 128-token chunks, opportunistic small batching inside the host process to amortize kernel launches. Intentionally trades some addl latency for cost savings.
- MB (multiplexed bulk): aggregate many short requests into a larger batch on the host for kernel-level throughput; adds framing multiplexing and reassembly overhead but maximizes GPU utilization on steady load.

Summary table (single-run numbers, representative):
Mode | steady p50 | steady p90 | steady p99 | microburst p99 | cost /1k q | sustained qps (observed)
-----|------------:|-----------:|-----------:|--------------:|-----------:|---------------------:
FP   |  85 ms      | 140 ms     | 420 ms     |  1,100 ms     | $0.78     | 120 qps
CS   | 110 ms      | 210 ms     | 900 ms     |  2,500 ms     | $0.62     | 95 qps
MB   | 160 ms      | 300 ms     | 650 ms     |  1,200 ms     | $0.46     | 150 qps

Interpretation notes on the table:
- FP gives the best median (p50) and the lowest microburst amplification at p99; cost is higher because kernels cannot be as effectively amortized across many users.
- CS reduces steady-state cost materially (approx -20% vs FP) while keeping p50 close, but p99 under microbursts degrades sharply: chunk reassembly queues amplify tail latencies when ingress is spiky.
- MB achieves the best cost but increases median latency and is brittle during short, high-cardinality spikes because the batching frontier must either flush early (increasing cost) or wait (increasing p99). In our microburst test MB had lower microburst p99 than CS but still higher than FP.

ASCII latency-over-time sketch (steady then microburst at t=+6m, 5s spike):
Time(ms) legend: each "-" = 50 ms, "*" indicates p99 events
FP  : p50 [-------*------] p90 [-----------] p99 [-----------------*]
CS  : p50 [----------] p90 [----------------] p99 [----------------------------*]
MB  : p50 [---------------] p90 [---------------------] p99 [-------------------------*]
(visual only; spikes align with the 5s microburst region)

Resource/utilization observations:
- GPU occupancy: MB >> CS > FP during steady state (MB ~78% avg occupancy, CS ~60%, FP ~45%).
- CPU host time: FP < CS < MB for per-request framing and scheduling. MB shows higher host-side tail CPU latency during the microburst due to reassembly locks.
- KV cache hit effect: enabling prefix cache reduced p50 by ~15% across all modes; p99 reduction was most significant for FP (approx -120 ms) because FP was already low-overhead and effectively exploited cache hit fast paths.

Failure modes and platform implications:
- Microburst resilience: FP is the most robust to very short, high-card spikes because it avoids batching waits; CS suffers due to chunking queues; MB fails worst when the controller decides to hold batches expecting more requests (backpressure ripple).
- Cost-accounting: MB looks great on per-token cost for steady, high-utilization customers but can be misleading for bursty PLG usage where p99 is business-critical.
- Operational complexity: MB requires more careful admission control and adaptive batch timeouts; CS needs tighter per-connection flow control to avoid head-of-line blocking.

Quick actionables (short list):
1) Short-term (this sprint): enable adaptive early-flush for MB when ingress derivative > threshold (JIRA-PLAT-912). Run new microburst set to confirm p99 improvements.
2) Medium-term: instrument chunk reassembly queue depths and expose per-tenant chunk-latency SLI in console (owner: Samir).
3) Product: codify guidance in the docs: prefer FP for interactive consumer-facing features with strict p99 SLAs; recommend CS for sessionized clients with moderate cost sensitivity; recommend MB for high-throughput steady workloads (batching-friendly B2B APIs).
4) Research spike: test hybrid routing where short requests (<40 tokens) are forced into MB and longer chat generations go to FP — hypothesize ~10–15% cost savings without p99 regression. Schedule 2-day spike.

Open questions / uncertainties:
- How representative is the model used of our verified catalog? We used a single 16k open model; larger decoder-only architectures may change the balance.
- Does multi-tenant interference amplify MB tail beyond what we saw on single-slot nodes? Need cross-tenant synthetic test.
- Pricing model interaction: should we show customers a blended cost estimate when we auto-route between FP/CS/MB? UX/complexity tradeoff.

Appendix: minimal raw numbers (sampled)
- FP steady: avg latency 95 ms, p50 85, p90 140, p99 420, GPU-sec/request 0.00095 -> cost/1k q $0.78
- CS steady: avg latency 130 ms, p50 110, p90 210, p99 900, GPU-sec/request 0.00075 -> cost/1k q $0.62
- MB steady: avg latency 175 ms, p50 160, p90 300, p99 650, GPU-sec/request 0.00055 -> cost/1k q $0.46

Notes-to-self / next experiment checklist:
- Run the same three modes on a smaller model (7B) and on a larger 70B to compare kernel launch amortization scaling.
- Add end-to-end client-side jitter (simulated real-world mobile) to the microburst tests.
- Measure effect of adding short (50ms) fixed per-request admission token in FP to see if we can artificially increase amortization without batching.

If you read this and want numbers or CSV export, tell me which bucket (steady/microburst/sessionized) and I'll paste raw CSV from the harness.

-- Aisha
